question: What does the intraperitoneal (IP) route actually mean?

options.A: Infusing fluids directly into a large peripheral vein
options.B: Swallowing drugs that dissolve in the stomach lining
options.C: Placing medicated patches onto the abdominal skin
options.D: Injecting medication directly into the peritoneal cavity

explanation: Great job! The intraperitoneal route simply means putting medication straight into the peritoneal cavity that surrounds your belly organs. Think of it as a direct shortcut to the abdominal space! [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h1)

question: In which hospital units are nurses most likely to use the intraperitoneal route?
explanation: Spot on! You'll mostly see IP administration when caring for kidney patients doing peritoneal dialysis or cancer patients receiving special belly chemotherapy. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h1)

question: How would you best describe the peritoneum?

options.A: A thick muscular wall separating the chest and belly
options.B: The outermost layer of the human heart muscle
options.C: The primary filtering unit inside human kidneys
options.D: A serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity

explanation: You've got this! The peritoneum is a smooth, slippery lining that wraps around your tummy wall and internal organs, keeping everything neatly cushioned. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h2)

question: Why is the large surface area of the peritoneal cavity so useful in medical care?

options.A: It prevents any medication from entering the systemic bloodstream
options.B: It stores excess fat to protect organs from physical trauma
options.C: It completely stops bacteria from causing localized infections
options.D: It provides a wide space for efficient fluid and drug exchange

explanation: Exactly! Because the peritoneal membrane is so wide and full of tiny blood vessels, it acts like a giant sponge, making it easy to swap fluids and medicines in and out. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h2)

question: What is the biggest perk of giving chemotherapy drugs through the intraperitoneal route?

options.A: It delivers a high concentration of the drug directly to abdominal tumors
options.B: It allows the liver to break down the medicine before it works
options.C: It makes the drug absorb instantly into the brain tissue
options.D: It completely prevents the drug from ever reaching the bloodstream

explanation: Brilliant! By putting chemo straight into the belly, you give the tumor a powerful, direct bath of medicine right where it lives. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h3)

question: Through which tiny pathways do drugs leave the peritoneal cavity and enter the body?

options.C: Bile ducts and the gall bladder

explanation: Correct! The web of tiny blood capillaries and lymph channels in the peritoneal membrane helps pick up the drugs and carry them where they need to go. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h3)

question: Which kidney condition frequently relies on the intraperitoneal route for daily management?
explanation: You nailed it! Peritoneal dialysis uses the patient's own belly lining as a natural filter when their kidneys can no longer clean the blood. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h4)

question: A patient with advanced ovarian cancer receives a drug infused right into her abdomen. Why choose this route?

options.A: To bypass the digestive tract because the patient cannot swallow
options.B: To target cancer cells locally within the peritoneal space
options.C: To rapidly correct severe dehydration and electrolyte loss
options.D: To provide immediate pain relief through spinal nerve blocks

explanation: Spot on! Delivering the medication straight to the peritoneal space attacks those ovarian cancer cells right where they are grouped. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h4)

question: Why do nurses always warm up peritoneal dialysis fluids before infusing them?

options.A: To kill any bacteria present in the plastic tubing
options.B: To prevent abdominal cramping and patient hypothermia
options.C: To prevent the fluid from turning into a solid gel
options.D: To make the drug dissolve faster inside the IV bag

explanation: Exactly! Putting cold fluid straight into the belly causes painful cramps and can drop the patient's body temperature. Always warm it to body temperature first! [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h5)

question: What is a vital nursing duty when managing a patient on peritoneal fluid exchange?

options.A: Checking the patient's blood pressure every five minutes
options.B: Disconnecting the sterile tubing system every two hours
options.C: Accurately recording the volume of fluid in and out
options.D: Massaging the patient's abdomen firmly to speed drainage

explanation: You got it! Keeping a strict fluid balance chart ensures the patient is draining out everything they put in and helps catch blockages early. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h5)

question: What are the classic warning signs of peritonitis in a patient getting IP therapy?

options.A: A high fever accompanied by a persistent dry cough
options.B: Sudden swelling and redness of the lower legs
options.C: Cloudy effluent drainage and severe abdominal pain
options.D: Complete inability to speak or swallow food

explanation: Spot on! If the drained fluid looks cloudy instead of clear, paired with bad belly pain, it's a huge red flag for peritonitis (infection). [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a typical complication of intraperitoneal administration?
explanation: Correct! Inhalation pneumonia is a lung issue, so it's not a direct local complication of accessing the peritoneal belly cavity. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h6)

question: What is a major plus of using the intraperitoneal route instead of pills for belly issues?

options.A: It completely avoids the need for any sterile equipment or supplies
options.B: It allows patients to self-administer complex chemotherapy at home
options.C: It delivers higher local drug concentrations directly to the target area
options.D: It eliminates all risks of systemic side effects and infection

explanation: Brilliant! Going straight to the source means the medication hits the problem area hard and fast, way better than waiting for a pill to digest. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h7)

question: What is the biggest downside or risk linked to the intraperitoneal route?

options.A: High risk of infection and peritonitis
options.B: Complete failure of the human respiratory system
options.C: Permanent paralysis of the skeletal muscles
options.D: Instantaneous destruction of all oral medications

explanation: You got it! Anytime you open up or access the sterile peritoneal cavity, germs can sneak in, making infection and peritonitis the main danger to watch for. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T11#GNS125_U3_T11_h7)
